title: Anatomy and Physiology for Nurses
description: An integrated overview of the body systems for School/College of Nursing students: skeleton and muscles, heart and blood, lungs, digestion, kidneys, nerves and hormones.

topics.title: Skeletal and Muscular Systems
topics.summary: Bones of the skeleton, types of joints and skeletal muscles.

notes.b: The adult skeleton has 206 bones, divided into the axial skeleton (skull, vertebral column, ribs and sternum — 80 bones) and the appendicular skeleton (limbs and girdles — 126 bones). The vertebral column has 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 fused sacral and about 4 fused coccygeal vertebrae. The femur is the longest and strongest bone; the stapes in the middle ear is the smallest. Functions of bone: support, protection, movement, blood cell formation (red marrow) and mineral storage (calcium, phosphate).
k: Vertebrae: 7 C, 12 T, 5 L, 5 S, 4 Co

notes.b: Joints are fibrous (immovable, e.g. skull sutures), cartilaginous (slightly movable, e.g. intervertebral discs, pubic symphysis) or synovial (freely movable, e.g. knee, hip, shoulder). Synovial joints have a joint capsule, synovial membrane and synovial fluid. The body has three muscle types: skeletal (voluntary), cardiac and smooth (involuntary). Common injection muscles are the deltoid, gluteus medius (ventrogluteal site) and vastus lateralis.
k: Knee and hip are synovial joints

Adults have 206 bones; babies have more that later fuse.

The femur (thigh bone) is the longest and strongest.

topics.title: The Heart, Blood and Circulation
topics.summary: Structure of the heart, blood flow through the heart, blood vessels and blood components.

notes.b: The heart has four chambers: right and left atria and right and left ventricles. Deoxygenated blood from the body enters the right atrium via the superior and inferior venae cavae, passes through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, then through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary artery to the lungs. Oxygenated blood returns via the pulmonary veins to the left atrium, through the mitral (bicuspid) valve to the left ventricle, then through the aortic valve into the aorta. The left ventricle has the thickest wall. The heart is supplied by the coronary arteries.
k: RA → tricuspid → RV → pulmonary artery → lungs
Pulmonary veins → LA → mitral → LV → aorta

notes.b: Arteries carry blood away from the heart (all carry oxygenated blood except the pulmonary artery); veins return blood to the heart and have valves; capillaries are where exchange takes place. Blood consists of plasma (~55%) and cells (~45%): red cells carry oxygen with haemoglobin, white cells fight infection and platelets help clotting. An adult has about 5 litres of blood. Normal pulse is 60–100 beats per minute and normal blood pressure about 120/80 mmHg.

q: Which chamber of the heart receives blood from the venae cavae?
The superior and inferior venae cavae empty into the right atrium.
The valve between the left atrium and left ventricle is the:
The mitral valve has two cusps.
Which blood vessel carries deoxygenated blood away from the heart?
The pulmonary artery takes deoxygenated blood to the lungs.
The chamber with the thickest muscular wall is the:
The left ventricle pumps blood to the whole body.
Exchange of gases and nutrients with tissues takes place in the:
Capillary walls are one cell thick.
Blood vessels that contain valves to prevent backflow are:
Venous valves help return blood against gravity.
The blood cells that help in clotting are:
Platelets form plugs and support coagulation.
The normal adult resting pulse rate is:
A resting pulse of 60–100 bpm is normal.

topics.title: The Respiratory System
topics.summary: Airways, lungs, mechanism of breathing and gas exchange.

notes.b: Air passes through the nose (warmed, moistened, filtered), pharynx, larynx (voice box, protected by the epiglottis during swallowing), trachea, right and left bronchi, bronchioles and finally the alveoli, where gas exchange occurs. The right lung has three lobes and the left two. The lungs are covered by pleura. Cilia and mucus trap and sweep out particles.
k: Nose → pharynx → larynx → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli
Epiglottis prevents food entering the airway

notes.b: During inspiration the diaphragm contracts and flattens and the intercostal muscles lift the ribs, enlarging the chest so air flows in; expiration is usually passive. Oxygen diffuses from alveoli into blood and carbon dioxide from blood into alveoli. The normal adult respiratory rate is 12–20 breaths per minute. Carbon dioxide level in blood is the main stimulus for breathing, controlled by the respiratory centre in the medulla oblongata.

q: Gas exchange in the lungs takes place in the:
Alveoli have thin walls surrounded by capillaries.
The structure that prevents food from entering the trachea is the:
The epiglottis covers the larynx during swallowing.
How many lobes does the left lung have?
The left lung has two lobes; the right has three.

The larynx contains the vocal cords.

The respiratory centre is in the brainstem medulla.

Adults normally breathe 12–20 times per minute.

topics.title: Digestive and Urinary Systems
topics.summary: Organs of digestion, the liver and pancreas, and the kidneys and urine formation.

notes.b: The digestive tract runs from mouth to anus: mouth (chewing, salivary amylase), oesophagus, stomach (acid and pepsin), small intestine (duodenum, jejunum, ileum — main site of digestion and absorption, with villi), large intestine (absorbs water and forms faeces) and rectum. Accessory organs: salivary glands, liver (makes bile, stores glycogen, detoxifies drugs, makes plasma proteins and clotting factors), gallbladder (stores bile), and pancreas (digestive enzymes and the hormones insulin and glucagon).
k: Liver makes bile; gallbladder stores it

notes.b: The urinary system consists of two kidneys, two ureters, the bladder and the urethra. The functional unit of the kidney is the nephron (about one million per kidney), which filters blood in the glomerulus and reabsorbs useful substances in the tubules. Kidneys remove waste (urea, creatinine), balance water and electrolytes, regulate blood pressure (renin), stimulate red cell production (erythropoietin) and activate vitamin D. Normal adult urine output is at least 0.5 mL/kg/hour (about 1–2 L/day); less than 400 mL/day is oliguria.

topics.title: Nervous and Endocrine Systems
topics.summary: Brain, spinal cord, nerves, reflexes and the major endocrine glands.

notes.b: The central nervous system is the brain and spinal cord; the peripheral nervous system includes 12 pairs of cranial nerves and 31 pairs of spinal nerves. The cerebrum controls thought, voluntary movement and sensation; the cerebellum coordinates balance and movement; the brainstem (midbrain, pons, medulla) controls breathing and heart rate. The autonomic nervous system has sympathetic ('fight or flight') and parasympathetic ('rest and digest') divisions. A reflex arc (receptor → sensory neuron → spinal cord → motor neuron → effector) produces rapid involuntary responses such as the knee jerk. The Glasgow Coma Scale (3–15) assesses consciousness.

Endocrine glands secrete hormones into the blood. The pituitary ('master gland') is controlled by the hypothalamus and secretes growth hormone, TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH, prolactin (anterior) and ADH and oxytocin (posterior). The thyroid produces thyroxine (metabolic rate; iodine deficiency causes goitre). The parathyroids regulate calcium. The adrenal cortex secretes cortisol and aldosterone; the adrenal medulla secretes adrenaline. The pancreas secretes insulin (lowers glucose) and glucagon (raises glucose). The ovaries and testes secrete sex hormones.
k: Insulin lowers, glucagon raises blood glucose
